title: Mathematics AI HL - Set D - Paper 2

questions.stem: A workshop models weekly demand for a product as $q(p)=500e^{-0.04p}$, where $p$ is the selling price in dollars, $0\le p\le100$. Every demanded unit can initially be supplied. Each unit costs \$8 to make and fixed weekly costs are \$1200. The expected weekly profit is revenue minus all production and fixed costs.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Optimize profit rather than revenue, use the permitted domain and then activate a capacity constraint.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the profit function $\Pi(p)$ and find its derivative.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the price giving maximum expected profit, and the corresponding demand and profit. Justify the maximum on the stated domain.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the interval of prices giving non-negative expected profit.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Production capacity is reduced to $100$ units per week. The workshop chooses a price at which the modelled demand does not exceed capacity. Find the price maximizing expected profit under this restriction, and its profit.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: If only fixed weekly costs increase, explain how the unconstrained profit-maximizing price and the set of profitable prices are affected.

steps.text: Revenue is $pq(p)$ and variable cost is $8q(p)$.
Differentiate using the product rule.
The derivative changes from positive to negative there, so it gives the global maximum on $[0,100]$.
Demand is $133.5677$ units and profit is \$2139.191.
Solve $500(p-8)e^{-0.04p}=1200$ numerically on the given domain.
The two roots are $11.85636$ and $87.51051$ dollars.
The profit is non-negative between and including these roots.
The smallest feasible price is $40.23595$ dollars, above $33$.
The profit function is decreasing throughout the new feasible interval, so choose this boundary price.
The maximum feasible expected profit is \$2023.595.
A change in fixed costs shifts the profit function vertically without changing its derivative.
The unconstrained maximizing price remains $33$, provided the demand and variable-cost models are unchanged.
The range of prices with non-negative profit shrinks, and could disappear if fixed costs exceed the maximum contribution before fixed costs.

questions.answerSummary: $\Pi\prime(p)=500e^{-0.04p}\{1-0.04(p-8)\}$.; Demand is $133.5677$ units and profit is \$2139.191.; The profit is non-negative between and including these roots.; The maximum feasible expected profit is \$2023.595.; The range of prices with non-negative profit shrinks, and could disappear if fixed costs exceed the maximum contribution before fixed costs.

questions.stem: A weather model has states sunny $(S)$ and rainy $(R)$. In either state, the probability of staying in that state on the next day is $0.75$. Day $0$ is sunny. A solar unit produces $10$ kWh on a sunny day and $3$ kWh on a rainy day. The Markov state for each day determines that day's production. Let $p_n=P(\text{day }n\text{ is sunny})$.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Distinguish marginal state probabilities, dependent paths and linearity of expectation in a cumulative energy model.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the transition matrix using column state vectors ordered $(S,R)$, and show that $p_{n+1}=0.5p_n+0.25$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: By considering $p_n-0.5$, obtain an explicit expression for $p_n$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the steady-state distribution and explain why this chain has a unique long-run distribution.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Find the probability that exactly two of days $1,2,3$ are sunny.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Find the expected total energy produced over days $1$ to $10$, showing a geometric sum.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain why it would be incorrect to model the number of sunny days among days $1,2,3$ as $\operatorname{Bin}(3,0.5)$.

steps.text: $T=\begin{pmatrix}0.75&0.25\\0.25&0.75\end{pmatrix}$.
This simplifies to $0.5p_n+0.25$.
This is geometric, with initial value $p_0-0.5=0.5$.
The steady state is $(0.5,0.5)^T$.
All entries of $T$ are positive, so the chain is regular.
The possible paths are $SSR,SRS,RSS$, starting from sunny day $0$.
Add these mutually exclusive path probabilities.
The total probability is $0.234375$.
The expectation for day $n$ is $10p_n+3(1-p_n)=6.5+3.5(0.5)^n$.
Sum over $n=1,\ldots,10$, using linearity of expectation even though days are dependent.
The expected energy is $68.49658$ kWh.
The day states are dependent: for example $P(S_{n+1}\mid S_n)=0.75$, not $0.5$.
Also the marginal probabilities for the first three days are not all $0.5$, because the process starts sunny.

questions.answerSummary: This simplifies to $0.5p_n+0.25$.; $p_n=0.5+0.5(0.5)^n$.; All entries of $T$ are positive, so the chain is regular.; The total probability is $0.234375$.; The expected energy is $68.49658$ kWh.; Also the marginal probabilities for the first three days are not all $0.5$, because the process starts sunny.

questions.stem:
An environmental scientist records independent pairs of water temperature $x$ in degrees Celsius and dissolved oxygen $y$ in mg per litre from eight randomly selected comparable sites. For the correlation test, assume the population of pairs is bivariate normal.

| $x$ | 12 | 14 | 16 | 18 | 20 | 22 | 24 | 26 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | 10.4 | 9.8 | 9.7 | 8.8 | 8.6 | 8.2 | 7.9 | 7.4 |
questions.cognitiveDemand: Compare Pearson and rank evidence, apply a declared one-sided population correlation test, and diagnose a leverage point.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find Pearson's correlation coefficient and the least-squares regression line of $y$ on $x$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: At the $1\%$ significance level, test whether the population correlation is negative. State hypotheses and report an appropriate test statistic, degrees of freedom, $p$-value and conclusion.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find Spearman's rank correlation coefficient and explain why it differs from Pearson's coefficient here.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Predict dissolved oxygen at $21^\circ$C and find the residual for the observed site at $20^\circ$C.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A ninth recorded pair is $(40,12)$. Find the new Pearson coefficient. Discuss whether the extra observation should automatically be deleted and whether the original correlation establishes a causal effect of temperature.

steps.text: Use the eight raw pairs to fit $y=a+bx$.
The fitted line is $y=12.83095+(-0.2095238)x$.
Pearson's coefficient is $r=-0.9903281$.
Use a correlation $t$ test on the given raw bivariate-normal pairs.
$t=r\sqrt{(8-2)/(1-r^2)}=-17.48383$, with $6$ degrees of freedom.
The lower-tail $p$-value is $1.122767\times10^{-6}$.
Reject $H_0$ at $1\%$; there is evidence of a negative population correlation under these assumptions.
Temperatures strictly increase while oxygen values strictly decrease, giving reverse ranks without ties.
Spearman's coefficient is $-1$.
The ordering is perfectly decreasing, but the points do not lie exactly on a straight line; Pearson measures linear association rather than only rank order.
Substitute into the fitted line, and take residual as observed minus predicted.
The prediction at $21^\circ$C is $8.430952$ mg per litre.
The residual at $20^\circ$C is $8.6-8.640476=-0.04047619$ mg per litre.
Recalculate Pearson's coefficient using all nine pairs.
The new coefficient is $r=0.246713$.
The point has strong influence, but deletion requires investigation of measurement validity and population comparability, not merely dislike of its effect.
Observational association alone does not establish causation; other site conditions may affect oxygen.

questions.answerSummary: Pearson's coefficient is $r=-0.9903281$.; Reject $H_0$ at $1\%$; there is evidence of a negative population correlation under these assumptions.; The ordering is perfectly decreasing, but the points do not lie exactly on a straight line; Pearson measures linear association rather than only rank order.; The residual at $20^\circ$C is $8.6-8.640476=-0.04047619$ mg per litre.; Observational association alone does not establish causation; other site conditions may affect oxygen.

questions.stem:
A transport researcher independently samples $60$ residents at random within each of three zones. Each resident reports one main travel mode. No resident appears twice. The observed counts are:

| Zone | Bus | Walk | Cycle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 30 | 20 | 10 |
| 2 | 18 | 25 | 17 |
| 3 | 12 | 15 | 33 |

 The three zones have different population sizes; equal sample sizes were chosen for convenience.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Analyze association, identify its main contribution and distinguish a conditional association study from a population-wide estimate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Under independence of zone and travel mode, find the expected-frequency table and check the expected-count condition.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Carry out a chi-square independence test at the $5\%$ significance level. State hypotheses, degrees of freedom, statistic, $p$-value and conclusion.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify the single cell making the largest contribution to the statistic. Calculate that contribution and interpret the direction of its deviation.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Zones 2 and 3 are combined into one category. Repeat the independence test for the resulting $2\times3$ table and state whether the conclusion changes.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain why the pooled sample proportion travelling by bus need not estimate the whole area's bus-use proportion accurately. Give a suitable adjustment if zone population sizes are known.

steps.text: Expected count is row total times column total divided by $180$.
Every row and column total is $60$, so all nine expected counts are $20$.
Each expected count is greater than $5$, satisfying the stated chi-square condition.
$H_0$: travel mode and zone are independent; $H_1$: they are associated.
Calculate $\sum(O-E)^2/E$ over all nine cells.
The upper-tail $p$-value is $5.518909\times10^{-5}$.
Reject $H_0$ at $5\%$; there is evidence of an association between zone and travel mode.
Compare the squared standardized deviations $(O-20)^2/20$.
Zone 3, cycle has the largest contribution, $13^2/20=8.45$.
Cycling is more frequent in the Zone 3 sample than expected under independence.
The new rows are $(30,20,10)$ and $(30,40,50)$, with expected rows $(20,20,20)$ and $(40,40,40)$.
Use the new table and $df=(2-1)(3-1)=2$.
The null is still rejected at $5\%$; the binary zone grouping remains associated with travel mode.
The pooled sample gives each zone equal weight because each contributes $60$ observations.
The zone populations are unequal, so this need not match residents' actual distribution across zones.
Establish the estimated bus fraction within each zone.
Weight those fractions by the respective zone population proportions, rather than averaging the three fractions equally.

questions.answerSummary: Each expected count is greater than $5$, satisfying the stated chi-square condition.; Reject $H_0$ at $5\%$; there is evidence of an association between zone and travel mode.; Cycling is more frequent in the Zone 3 sample than expected under independence.; The null is still rejected at $5\%$; the binary zone grouping remains associated with travel mode.; Weight those fractions by the respective zone population proportions, rather than averaging the three fractions equally.

questions.stem: A damped displacement $x(t)$ satisfies the given equation $x\prime\prime+3x\prime+2x=0$, with $x(0)=4$ and $x\prime(0)=-2$. Displacement is in centimetres and time is in seconds. Let $v=x\prime$. The model is used only for $t\ge0$.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Convert the supplied second-order model, use distinct real eigendirections and distinguish simultaneous from sequential numerical updates.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the model as a first-order matrix system for $(x,v)^T$, including its initial state.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors of the system matrix. Classify the equilibrium at the origin.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Use the eigensolutions and initial state to find $x(t)$ and $v(t)$.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Show that the displacement remains positive and decreases for all $t\ge0$. Explain what the model predicts in the long term.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Use Euler's method on the coupled first-order system, with step size $0.2$ seconds, to estimate the state at $t=0.4$. Compare it with the exact state. Both updates at a step must use the same old state.

steps.text: $x\prime=v$.
$v\prime=-2x-3v$, so $\binom{x\prime}{v\prime}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&-3\end{pmatrix}\binom{x}{v}$.
The initial state is $(4,-2)^T$.
$\det(M-\lambda I)=\lambda^2+3\lambda+2$.
The eigenvalues are $-1,-2$.
Corresponding eigenvectors are $(1,-1)^T$ and $(1,-2)^T$.
The distinct negative real eigenvalues give a stable node.
The initial conditions give $A+B=4$ and $-A-2B=-2$.
Solving gives $A=6$, $B=-2$.
$v=e^{-t}(-6+4e^{-t})<0$ on the same domain.
Both exponentials tend to zero, so the displacement decreases toward zero without crossing it.
Use $x_{n+1}=x_n+0.2v_n$, $v_{n+1}=v_n+0.2(-2x_n-3v_n)$ simultaneously. The first state is $(3.6,-2.4)$.
After the second step the Euler state is $(3.12,-2.4)$.
The exact state is $(3.123262,-2.224604)$; Euler slightly understates $x$ and makes the velocity more negative.

questions.answerSummary: The initial state is $(4,-2)^T$.; The distinct negative real eigenvalues give a stable node.; $v(t)=-6e^{-t}+4e^{-2t}$.; Both exponentials tend to zero, so the displacement decreases toward zero without crossing it.; The exact state is $(3.123262,-2.224604)$; Euler slightly understates $x$ and makes the velocity more negative.

questions.stem: Three emergency posts are at $A(0,0)$, $B(8,0)$ and $C(4,6)$, with coordinates in kilometres. The service region is exactly the closed triangular region $ABC$. Straight-line distance determines the nearest post. A transmitter is to be placed as far as possible from its nearest post while remaining in this triangle. For a convex polygonal cell, you may use the fact that the maximum distance from its site occurs at a cell vertex.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Solve a bounded largest-empty-circle problem and verify the interior optimum against all boundary candidates.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $AC$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the common Voronoi vertex and its distance from each post. Check that it lies inside the triangle.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the area of the portion of the triangle allocated to post $A$.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Find the transmitter's optimal position and the maximum distance from its nearest post. Justify the global optimum by checking all types of cell vertex, including those on the triangle boundary.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The transmitter must instead be on the base road $AB$. Find its best position and maximum nearest-post distance.

steps.text: The bisector of horizontal $AB$ passes through $(4,0)$.
It is $x=4$.
The second bisector is $2x+3y=13$.
Intersect $x=4$ and $2x+3y=13$.
The vertex is $V=(4,5/3)$.
The common distance is $\sqrt{16+25/9}=13/3$ km.
At $x=4$ the triangle extends from $y=0$ to $y=6$, so $V$ is inside.
The cell is the polygon with vertices $(0,0),(4,0),(4,5/3),(2,3)$.
The final point is the midpoint of side $AC$, where its bisector meets the triangle boundary.
Use a polygon area formula or divide the region into triangles.
The area is $23/3\ \mathrm{km}^2$.
The cell vertices consist of the posts themselves, the three side midpoints, and $V$.
Nearest distances there are $0$, $4$ at the midpoint of $AB$, $\sqrt{13}$ at the other two midpoints, and $13/3$ at $V$.
The supplied convex-cell maximum property means no interior or edge point within any cell can exceed its largest vertex distance.
The global optimum is $V=(4,5/3)$, with nearest-post distance $13/3$ km.
On $y=0$, the nearest of $A,B$ is at most $4$ km away, with equality only at $(4,0)$; $C$ is then $6$ km away.
The optimum is $(4,0)$ and the maximum nearest-post distance is $4$ km.

questions.answerSummary: The second bisector is $2x+3y=13$.; At $x=4$ the triangle extends from $y=0$ to $y=6$, so $V$ is inside.; The area is $23/3\ \mathrm{km}^2$.; The global optimum is $V=(4,5/3)$, with nearest-post distance $13/3$ km.; The optimum is $(4,0)$ and the maximum nearest-post distance is $4$ km.
